explanation: Third order neurons in sensory pathways start in the VPL nucleus of the thalamus and project via internal capsule to the primary somatosensory cortex (areas 3, 1, 2).
The gracile fasciculus carries proprioception and fine touch from the lower body (sacral, lumbar, and lower thoracic dermatomes) and synapses in the gracile nucleus.
The cuneate fasciculus carries proprioception and fine touch from the upper body (cervical and upper thoracic dermatomes) and synapses in the cuneate nucleus.
The medial lemniscus arises from the upper closed medulla (after crossing as internal arcuate fibers), not from the pons; it carries sensory information to the thalamus.
Proprioception encompasses the sensation of movement (kinesthesia), vibration, and joint/limb position, mediated by muscle spindles, tendon organs, and joint receptors.
Fine (discriminative) touch enables tactile localization and two-point discrimination, mediated by Meissner corpuscles and Merkel discs traveling via the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway.
Proprioception receptors include muscle spindles, tendon spindles (Golgi tendon organs), and joint receptors; Merkel discs are tactile receptors, not proprioceptive.
Fine touch receptors include Meissner corpuscles, Merkel discs, and Ruffini endings; tendon spindles are proprioceptive receptors, not tactile.
Gracile and cuneate tracts ascend ipsilaterally in the posterior columns before crossing in the medulla at the sensory decussation.
Proprioception fibers from the thalamus ascend via the posterior limb of the internal capsule (along with other sensory fibers) to the primary somatosensory cortex.
Crude (light) touch receptors include Meissner corpuscles, Merkel discs combined with free nerve endings, and peritrichial (hair follicle) nerve endings.
Crude touch uses medium-sized cells in dorsal root ganglia (not small), entering via the medial division of the posterior root, and ends in cortex area 3,1,2.
First order neurons for crude touch have cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia; their central processes enter the posterior root and ascend in the posterior column.
Second order neurons in the crude touch pathway start in the nucleus proprius (main sensory nucleus) of the spinal cord and ascend via the spinal lemniscus.
The ventral spinothalamic tract crosses at the spinal cord level and ascends through the brainstem, eventually reaching the thalamus via the spinal lemniscus.
The spinal lemniscus is formed by the union of ventral and lateral spinothalamic tracts, carrying pain and temperature sensation through the brainstem.
Free nerve endings are the receptors for pain and temperature sensation throughout the body; they are the most primitive and widely distributed sensory receptors.
Pain and temperature pathway uses small cells in dorsal root ganglia entering via the lateral division (not medium cells entering medially).
First order neurons for pain/temperature are small cells in dorsal root ganglia whose fibers enter via the lateral division of the posterior root and synapse in substantia gelatinosa.
The lateral spinothalamic tract arises from the opposite side (after crossing in the spinal cord) and ascends through all brainstem levels to the thalamus.
Second order neurons for pain/temperature start in the substantia gelatinosa (Roland's substance) of the posterior horn and ascend via the spinal lemniscus.
Facial proprioception uses unipolar neurons (no ganglia) with the mesencephalic nucleus as first order neuron; it is multipolar with proprioceptive ganglia, not sensory.
For facial touch, the first order neuron is in the trigeminal nucleus (mesencephalic for proprioception, principal sensory for touch) and the second order is the main sensory nucleus.
Pain and temperature from the face: first order neurons are in the trigeminal (spinal) nucleus, second order are in the spinal trigeminal nucleus that projects to the thalamus.
The trigeminal lemniscus (trigeminothalamic tract) carries facial sensory information (touch, pain, temperature) from the principal sensory and spinal trigeminal nuclei to the VPM thalamus.
The dorsal spinocerebellar tract carries impulses from the lower limb and trunk on the ipsilateral side (after crossing once in the spinal cord via Clarke's nucleus).
The ventral spinocerebellar tract carries impulses from the lower limb on both sides (decussates twice) and trunk on the same side, not only trunk on same side.
The dorsal spinocerebellar tract enters via the inferior cerebellar peduncle while the ventral spinocerebellar tract enters via the superior cerebellar peduncle.
The spinotectal tract arises from posterior horn cells (laminae I, V), ascends contralaterally to the superior colliculus for reflex eye/head movements, not the inferior olivary nucleus.
The spino-olivary tract ascends to the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla to mediate cerebellar climbing fiber input for motor learning, not eye/head reflexes.
The sulcomarginal tract is a descending motor tract in the anterior column, not a paired bilateral tract like vestibulospinal, reticulospinal, and tectospinal.
The tectospinal tract is a single midline tract (decussates in the midbrain); the other tracts (rubro-spinal, olivo-spinal) are also single but have bilateral components.
Lateral reticulospinal and rubrospinal tracts are indirect (multineuronal) tracts, while olivespinal, vestibulospinal, ventral reticulospinal, and sulcomarginal are direct.
The tectospinal tract arises from the superior colliculus of the midbrain tectum and descends to control reflexive head and neck movements in response to visual stimuli.
Rubrospinal and ventral vestibulospinal tracts do NOT extend to all spinal levels; lateral vestibulospinal, sulcomarginal, and reticulospinal do.
